The content covers topics in linear algebra, including more on concepts on space and isomerism. However, the exam covers no difficult materials and is even easier than MATH2111 in my opinion. After eliminating the parts that are not covered in exam, this course nearly taught nothing at all, even though the lecture notes provide are actually good.

As a physics major student study QM before linear algebra, I expected this course covers the complex part but unfortunately it did not.

1. System of Linear Equations
2. Euclidean Space

Some excluded topic: block matrix, isomorphosim, complex linear algebra, inner product, geometry of determinant, quardratic form, complex orthogonal diagonalisation
sections.teaching: Prof. YAN explains the content of lecture notes, including the 'excluded part' very clearly. Unfortunately he spent too much time on explaining simple content and he did not emphasize on the difficult part and ignored them for this course.
sections.grading:
ABCDE cannot be used to describe how the grading was in this course. The mean is way too high and the exams are way too easy, even comparing to high school standard. Knowing linear algebra grants you at least A-, but to get A/A+, you should be good at not making careless mistakes. I understand Prof. YAN's concern on distributing too many A+/A, but the marks deduction of final exam can be described as unfair for making minor mistakes.

For Final Exam, Prof. YAN deducts 5 marks for each, including copying wrong matrix as the answer (all steps correct btw), and one mistake can eliminate the chance of getting A+. I would say the exam is too easy but the grading does not truly reflect students' abilties.

sections.content:
Before midterm it covers three equivalent concepts: system of linear equations, Euclidean space and linear transformation (Ch 1 - 3).

After midterm it covers vector space (which is generalization of Ch 1 - 3 from Euclidean space to vector space), orthogonalization, determinant (yes, that late), spectral theory.

There are a lot of content but they are not deep, basically you could ace the course just knowing how to compute this and that. The 'proof' exercises are usually not very rigorous either. However, it seems Marberg would return teaching this course when his sabbatical is over (according to YM).

If you really want to learn Linear Algebra properly, please read Linear Algebra Done Right and 3blue1brown's Essence of linear algebra series as others suggested, especially the latter will save you a lot of time on getting the right intuition and thinking of linear algebra concept.
sections.teaching:
Skipped most of the lectures after midterm, but from my experience before midterm, his teaching is not too bad. But once again, content is quite shallow. Speaking of which, he is a very chill prof, others say he gives break once every 20 minutes, I say he gives that once every 10 mins for about 3 mins. No wait he won't be 'seriously lagging behind' as claimed later in the course LOL.

Too many typos in the notes, but he would clarify timely on WeChat group when someone asked. He is also generous in giving deadline extension (the last HW was extended by 1 whole week)
sections.grading:
Too good, it's a non-honor course difficulty in honor course grading standard. He kept his promise of setting 85 as cutoff of A-range, 60 as cutoff of B-range, and 34.xx for C-range. 47% got A- or above and 87% got B- or above.

Only 3 questions are marked and worth 10 points each, the others are graded by completion and worth 3 points each. Under this principle, basically at least 50% of the points are secured if you complete your homework. Due to his extremely simple solution in marking scheme, you can expect grading to be lenient too even for the graded problems.

He chooses basically the easiest topics to be in midterm and final. Before the final exam, he announced list of complicated/ more advanced topics that will not be included in the exam. In the final exam, a question asking for a R^2 vector satisfying two orthogonal projection criterion is worth 25 points. You can even look it up on your notes (open book exam) if you forgot/ didn't revise the concept, it's somewhere in the notes.
sections.workload: Maybe a little heavy, 1 assignment per week in principle. But the questions are still easy, good way to practice for your exams in my opinion. Ask/ wait for someone to ask for a homework deadline extension and continue. Based on past experience, the range of extended days goes from 3 days to 1 whole week.

Professor Yanmin is an excellent instructor. He’s very patient, approachable, and always encourages students to ask questions during or after lectures. His teaching style is clear and organized — even when the material gets abstract, he manages to explain it in a way that feels intuitive and accessible.

What’s especially great about him is how he balances theory and practice. He gives intuitive explanations for difficult concepts like eigenvalues and subspaces, and then connects them to real applications. His lectures never feel rushed, and he often pauses to check if everyone understands. Many students say his explanations make them actually enjoy Linear Algebra.

Overall, Professor Yanmin is one of the best math instructors I’ve had. He makes a subject that many find difficult feel logical and even elegant.

There are no surprises — if you attend class and understand the weekly material, you will do well. sections.workload:
The workload is very reasonable. Homework sets are short and mainly computational, often with hints or example solutions included. You can easily finish them within an hour or two each week. There aren’t too many assignments, and they never feel overwhelming.

Because the course is so clearly taught, you don’t need to spend a lot of extra time self-studying. The balance between workload and learning is excellent — enough to practice, but not too much to stress you out.

Overall, Professor Yanmin’s Linear Algebra course is one of the best-taught and most enjoyable math classes. The workload is light, the grading is fair, and the teaching quality is top-tier. Highly recommended.

sections.workload:
There will be 10 assignments, usually released 1-2 weeks before deadline, and the deadline of each assignment is usually exactly 1 week after the previous one, so 1 assignment/week.
The assignments are in the form of practice problems with arround 13 long questions, around 1/3 to 1/2 of them will be marked with a * which will be more challenging and would not make in to the exam questions. You only have to choose 4 problems from them and to get full credit you just need to make a good-faith attempt on these 4 problems. However there is also extra credit points you can earn by finishing another 4 questions, these credits are harder to get as you have to finish the question correctly. Extra credit is not added to your assignment grade and is calculated differently, and the maximum extra credit you can receive is 5% of your total grade, so if you fail the exams it doesn't matter if you get full extra credit.
Since the TA will only mark the first 8 questions and ignore the rest if you complete more than 8, choose which questions you are solving wisely.
From what I know most of the students would choose to finish eight of them, and for me personally most question can be finished in less than an hour, harder/longer ones around 2-3 hours at most, so it is recommended not to be a deadline fighter, I usually spend 5 hours/day and finish the assignment in 2 days right after It was released on canvas.

MATH2121 introduces fundamental concepts in linear algebra. Although the course code starts with "2", it is actually very easy for year-1 Gaokao students and does not require much calculus knowledge, so feel confident to enroll in it with your MATH1013 or MATH1014 (you need to write a waiver).

Quite standard stuff in any linear algebra course. I will paste the schedule below if you are interested.

Week 1: Linear systems, row reduction to echelon form (reading: Sections 1.1-1.2)
Week 2: Vectors, matrix equations, linear independence (reading: Sections 1.3-1.5, 1.7)
Week 3: Linear independence, linear transformations (reading: Sections 1.7-1.9)
Week 4: Matrix multiplication, the inverse of a matrix (reading: Sections 2.1-2.3)
Week 5: Subspaces, bases, dimension (reading: Sections 2.4, 2.8-2.9)
Week 6: Determinants (reading: Sections 3.1-3.2)
Week 7: Vector spaces, midterm (reading: Sections 4.1-4.6)
Week 8: Eigenvectors, and eigenvalues (reading: Section 5.1)
Week 9: Similarity and diagonalisable matrices (reading: Sections 5.2-5.4)
Week 10: Complex eigenvalues, properties of eigenvalues (reading: Sections 5.5, 6.1)
Week 11: Inner products, orthogonality, and projections (reading: Sections 6.1-6.3)
Week 12: Gram-Schmidt process, least-squares problems (reading: Sections 6.4-6.6)
Week 13: Symmetric matrices, SVDs (reading: Sections 7.1, 7.4)

Overall, this is pretty much the required course if you want to do anything STEM related and I would advise you to really study hard for this course, not only get assinments and exams done but
really fully read through the topics cause they are really important. I found myself reviewing the materials in the following semester when I study for other topics.

Not hard to follow, and not shallow in terms of depth of content.

You may also change the "2021" in the URL to "2020"/"2019"/"2018"/"2017". Eric has a webpage for all these fall semesters that offers this course. sections.teaching:
Eric has a double major from stanford and a PHD from MIT, so clearly he is a genuis. His understading about math is definately at a stage where he can just say something, and that sentence can be and should be memorized as a theory for us.

This semester, due to the pandemic, they adopted mix-mode teaching. L1 is purely online and L2 is F2F. But whichever section you are enrolled in, you can always watch the recording posted on the public course website from L1 zoom recording.

Personally, I would say, it's better to watch his lectures online instead of attending the class F2F. Because:
    1. Generally speaking, his pace of voice is rather slow. And it's just so easy to get sleepy when listening to his voice. 1.5xx speed of zoom recording is a pefect speed for listening to his lectures. And as he is a native speaker of English, 1.5xx doesn't make his voice unclear. It's just the right speed I think.
     2. Someone in a prvious review said his lectures are like some very decent Youtube videos without a Pause Button. I can't agree more on that. But when you watch Zoom recording, there is a pause button. You can pause and write down something he said that can be and should be memorized as a theory for us. (which happens quite often for me)

Generally, his teaches by following the lecture notes (i.e. making annotations whlie explaing, giving examples from time to time, and give some verbal "Eric's theory") He also uses Julia to do some demo during the lecture to help us visualize and understand some concepts or have a look at some applications of certain content covered in the lecture. They won't be covered in exams but they sometimes do promt better visualization and understading. The Youtube Link I put in the Workload Section may help as well.

Overall the teaching is good. Especially the "Eric's theory" part.

Eric also set up a discord server for the whole class, where you can ask questions (either about homeworks, logistics, grading cutoffs, etc.) And his reply is rather quick. So it's qiute easy to reach him out side of class.

Oh let me add one more thing: ERIC IS SO FREEKING DAMN HANDSOME

This years midterm was clearly more difficult than pastpapers, so the mean was obviously lower. But the final was somewhat similar to past years in terms of difficulty.

Here's what Eric said after the midterm:
"Approximate letter grade cutoffs in terms of the midterm score are as follows :
A: above 52
B: between 36 and 52
C: between 20 and 35"

So you can see that he assigns A range for [mean+1sd,inf), B range for [mean,mean+1sd), C range for [mean-1sd, mean) .etc. So the grading is obviously very lenient, as you can get A range only by achieving mean+1sd in exams. You might only get B range in many other Math and Comp courses.

Very straightforward content in terms of linear algebra, and it was clear that Professor Marberg was not satisfied with doing traditional "2121 stuff".

It was very nice of him introducing Pluto notebooks in class demonstrating linear algebra concepts in the Julia programming language(which was hard to catch up for me at that time, but it was surely of great help in terms of facilitating understanding in practice).

Hence, the overall course material seems to be fruitful. And it was generally harder than most courses that are not honor I have taken so far.
sections.teaching:
The teaching, in both lectures and tutorials, are pretty good. The Professor explains things clearly and elaborate concepts with Pluto notebooks.
While in the tutorials, there are a huge amount of conceptual problems, in which the T/F I found the most useful.
sections.grading:
The grading seems fair to me, even if you are around mean in the midterm but still do good in the final you can get a fair grade(60% for final for us). And here is what the Professor said,
"For a rough idea of how scores compare to letter grades: as with the midterm, scores that range from the mean to a little more than one standard deviation above (respectively, below) the mean approximately correspond to B (respectively, C) letter grades. Scores more than one standard deviation above or below the mean approximately correspond to A and D letter grades."
sections.workload: Not really anything to do if just finishing 10 problems a week on WebWork. But it takes more time to practise many basic ideas taught in class. While for those more advanced Julia things, it takes more time for you to play with it yourself to grasp the idea.

Prof. Li is an excellent mathematician. In terms of linear algebra, he definitely possesses much knowledge. He is able to present every proof smooth and explain them well. However, sometimes he will become so excited and go beyond the syllabus. The major problem of him is that his voice is way too soft. It is not that easy to listen to his words.

He gave a review of the last lecture every time. This made us easier to follow. However, this also made the lecture became very tedious as you would feel like every time the content is the same. To some extent, this is the problem of the content as well. It seems like most things are very alike but just change of the terms.

sections.content:
Week 1: Linear systems, row reduction to echelon form (reading: Sections 1.1-1.2)
Week 2: Vectors, matrix equations, linear independence (reading: Sections 1.3-1.5, 1.7)
Week 3: Matrices as linear transformations, applications (reading: Sections 1.8-1.10)
Week 4: Matrix multiplication, the inverse of a matrix (reading: Sections 2.1-2.3)
Week 5: Subspaces, null and column space, dimension (reading: Sections 2.4, 2.8-2.9)
Week 6: Determinants (reading: Sections 3.1-3.2)
Week 7: Vector spaces, eigenvectors, and eigenvalues (reading: Sections 4.1-4.6, 5.1)
Week 8: Similarity and diagonalisable matrices (reading: Sections 5.2-5.4)
Week 9: Complex eigenvalues, properties of eigenvalues (reading: Sections 5.5, 6.1)
Week 10: Inner products, orthogonality, and projections (reading: Sections 6.1-6.3)
Week 11: Gram-Schmidt process, least-squares problems (reading: Sections 6.4-6.6)
Week 12: Symmetric matrices, singular value decompositions (reading: Sections 7.1, 7.4)

You will find the difficulty of the course in the last few weeks escalated quickly. But the content before mid-term are just things in M2 in high school.
sections.teaching: The professor teaches with heart and willing to spend time in the study break to organize a review lecture. He also likes answering student's question. The reason I give B is that he really just read out the things on the notes in the lectures.
sections.grading: The grading is extremely good. You can get an A range  if you get >75% overall, which is easy and so you can get an A if you get >1 sd higher than mean. The reason I give B is that the mid-term consists only 30% of the final grade and the final consists 60%, which tells you that the mid-term is not important at all.
sections.workload: 8~11 webwork questions per week, some of them are tedious and I used MatLab/Python/Symbol lab etc. to solve the questions or it would have cost me 3 more hours to finish it.

sections.teaching: I didn't like Prof. Huang's teaching at all. He kept jumping from topic to topic, and he would jump back to a topic if he realized he forgot to mention something. He also occasionally covers some advanced topics that are irrelevant to the course, and it just confuses me more. If you find it hard to follow his teaching, I would recommend using the textbook to learn by yourself, or asking the TA, since the TA explains the content very well.
sections.grading:
20% Homework, 80% Final
There are sample midterm and final exams, and there is also a midterm exam that does not count towards your final grade. I would recommend doing these practice exams anyways, since they are very useful in helping you prepare for the final.
The final exam questions were very straightforward and reasonable.
sections.workload: We had handwritten assignments every other week, but the questions did not take too much time, and they really helped me understand the content.

sections.content: The lecture covers linear equations in linear algebra, matrix algebra, determinants, vector spaces, eigenvalues and eigenvectors and orthogonality. The topics are not difficult to learn even for people with little or no knowledge of linear algebra, but understanding how each of the theorems work could be quite tricky. For eigenvectors and orthogonality, the lecture only covers the first one third of the whole chapter.
sections.teaching: The professor was very enthusiastic about the lecture, and I enjoyed the lecture. However, sometimes his lecture was quite difficult to understand especially when he tried to explain how to prove theorems that are complicated. There is 5 minute break at the middle of the lecture for allowing students to take a short break or go to the bathroom.
sections.grading: The mid term was 30% of the total grade, and it is very easy to get full marks. The average was around 32/35 for the mid term. The final was much more difficult than the midterm, but you can get high score if you spend enough time studying/reviewing the lecture. The final covers 60% of the total score, so it is very important to be well prepared for the final. The homework only covers 5% of the total grade, and it is very easy to get 100% on the homework.
sections.workload: The workload is very low, because webwork is basically all the homework that you'll get. Other than webwork, there was only one homework that was asking us to write proof for 3 statements, and it only takes a few hours to complete.  Since there is very little homework, self study and reviewing the lecture is very important for getting a good grade.

We all be in UST long enough to know UST has no real good professor.

Prof. Chang is an average one. His words are fairly understandable, and as a person he is quite funny. I like his sense of humor; he sometime tells some funny math jokes.

He tended to write a lot on the broad and use some unnecessarily large examples. The lecture are mostly focused on proofs, especially the second part of the course (i.e. after midterm), so the lectures can get fairly dense. Once you get lost, it is unlikely that you will be back on track again on that day's lecture. Though, for people who are interested in pure math, I guess the rigorous maths  might be able to provide some insights.

For Prof. Chang alone, I will give a B~B- for teaching. But what's really the problem is the TA.

I only went to the tutorial twice, and I never understood a single words from the TA.
sections.grading:
Unexpectedly good.

The midterm is like a piece of cake. Even the professor said he make it too easy. (the mean is 33/35...)

The final is a lot harder ( much harder than the webwork), but still doable. It consist of a series of free response questions, along with a few T/F and MC (with multiple answers) asking for concepts. No proof was on the exam.

Personally my biggest problem in that final is only time, but even though I left like one whole page blank (I left out one part on each problem), I still ended up with an A-.
sections.workload:
Webwork every week (typically 4~6 problems) and one written homework (proofs) in the middle of the semester.

The webworks are very easy, if you really know the material well, you can easily solve them all within 10~15 minutes. But be careful, these exercise will only provide you the very minimal practice on the material. I suggest you spend the time do some more yourself if you're aiming for high grades.

I will say Meng GuoWu is a moderate teacher only.
He will answer students' questions in details but he will use the terms that you need to have revision to know what he is saying.
He wrote so many things on the blackboard and not using the notes he put in the website that makes people hard to follow.
sections.grading:
I got above average 1sd in midterm and below half sd in final and I got B-.
Moderate grade and a bit fair.
You can bring notes in the exams and so it is good for you to take notes in class.
The instructor got some helpful points for the course in the website and make sure you also read it when you are study.
Midterm I got True false, multiple choice and short questions. Final got all long questions and I copied all the steps from my notes lol.
The exams are quite hard, maybe that is because I have the course in spring semester but not in fall.
